name: Tea tree oil body wash

lead: Tea tree oil body wash is used by people aiming for fresher-smelling, clearer body skin, including for body odor and body acne. It contains an essential oil distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves.

Its main component, terpinen-4-ol, shows antibacterial and antifungal activity in laboratory studies, and the idea is that fewer odor and acne bacteria means a cleaner smell and fewer blemishes. Clinical evidence is limited; a small early trial compared a 5% tea tree oil body wash with 4% nasal ointment to standard MRSA decolonization and found a nonsignificant trend favoring tea tree oil.

paras: People use it in place of regular body wash in the shower, often focusing on the back, chest and underarms, and keep it up as part of a routine. Many pair it with a moisturizer since cleansers can dry skin.
Skin irritation and allergic contact dermatitis are reported, and possible endocrine concerns in boys and men have been raised. Tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed.

angle.text: Tea tree oil wash is used as a natural antibacterial cleanser to cut odor and acne bacteria, leaving body skin fresher and clearer. Lab studies show antibacterial activity; trials for odor or appearance are absent.

lead: Tea tree oil body wash is a cleanser containing tea tree (melaleuca) oil, an essential oil distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves.[1] In grooming discussions it is used as a natural antibacterial wash, including for body odor and body acne.

Laboratory studies show antimicrobial activity, but clinical evidence is limited.[1] A small early trial compared a 5% tea tree oil body wash with 4% nasal ointment to standard MRSA decolonization and found a nonsignificant trend favoring tea tree oil.[2] Reported adverse effects include skin irritation and allergic contact dermatitis.[1]
infobox: Approved complementary medicine in Australia; not an approved drug in the US[1]

paras: A 2015 Cochrane review of acne therapies found one low-quality trial showing benefit over placebo.[1] The European Medicines Agency recognises traditional use for small superficial wounds and insect bites.[1]

Tea tree oil can cause irritation and allergic contact dermatitis, with risk rising as the oil oxidises.[1] It is highly toxic if swallowed.[1] A possible risk of breast enlargement in men and prepubertal children has been reported, and a 2018 NIEHS study found four constituents to be endocrine disruptors.[1]

A 2000 small trial compared a tea tree oil nasal ointment and 5% body wash with mupirocin and triclosan for MRSA carriage; the tea tree combination appeared to perform better but the difference was not statistically significant.[2] No studies were found testing tea tree body wash for body odor or appearance.

timeline.event: Commercial production begins in Australia, led by chemist Arthur Penfold.[1]
Small MRSA decolonization trial of tea tree oil nasal ointment and body wash published.[2]
